analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited 'soft money' contributions to national political parties and caps candidates' self-funding.
analysis.headline: The soft money ban was referred to the House Oversight Committee the day it was introduced in January 1997 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal campaign law to bar national party committees and congressional campaign committees from accepting 'soft money' — the unlimited, largely unreported contributions that wealthy donors, corporations, and unions gave to parties outside normal limits. It would channel party election activity back under the normal contribution limits and disclosure rules, while raising the limit on individual gifts to a candidate from $1,000 to $2,500 and capping how much of their own money a House candidate can spend at $100,000 per cycle. It was introduced January 21, 1997, referred to the House Oversight Committee the same day, and no further action was ever taken [S2][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want to know who is paying for elections: the bill would force nearly all party spending on federal elections back into the disclosed, limited contribution system. Candidates who rely on many small and mid-size donors would also gain relative ground, since the individual contribution limit would triple while big soft-money checks would disappear, and self-funded candidates could no longer buy a House seat with unlimited personal wealth.

how_it_helps.text: National party committees and congressional campaign committees could no longer solicit or accept contributions that bypass the limits, prohibitions, and reporting requirements of federal campaign law [S2][S3].

Party spending on federal elections — get-out-the-vote drives in presidential years, voter registration, generic campaign activity, and anything identifying or promoting a federal candidate — would become subject to the same limits and disclosure rules as ordinary contributions and expenditures [S3].
House candidates could contribute no more than $100,000 of their own money per election cycle, limiting the advantage of wealthy self-financed candidates [S2][S3].

The individual contribution limit to a candidate would rise to $2,500 while the multicandidate committee (PAC) limit would drop to $2,500, narrowing the gap between individual donors and organized PACs [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: National political party committees and congressional campaign committees would lose their soft-money pipeline, and the wealthy donors, corporations, and unions who wrote six- and seven-figure soft-money checks would lose their largest, least-regulated channel of influence over federal elections.

drawbacks.text: Raising the individual contribution limit from $1,000 to $2,500 triples what any one donor can give a candidate, a trade-off reform critics have long argued partially offsets a soft-money ban by steering more large money through the front door [S2][S3].
The bill covers party committees but does not address independent spending or issue advertising by outside groups, so money seeking to influence federal elections could migrate around the ban [S3].

Party committees argued that soft money funded voter registration and turnout work, so the ban would push that activity into other, less accountable channels — a concern the bill partially answers by creating regulated State Party Grassroots Funds, but not fully [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — bringing party soft money under the same limits and disclosure rules as everything else — is a genuine restraint on big-money influence in federal elections, and the self-funding cap addresses wealth advantage directly. The doubled-to-tripled individual limit is a real cost, and the bill leaves independent spending untouched, so it is a partial fix rather than a comprehensive one. Its fatal weakness was political, not structural: with a single sponsor and one cosponsor, it never had the support to get a committee hearing, let alone a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Oversight Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Clement introduced the Campaign Truth and Fairness Act of 1997 on January 21, 1997, with one Republican cosponsor [S1][S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on House Oversight, which had jurisdiction over campaign finance [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no further activity of any kind for the remaining two years of the Congress [S5].
The bill's provisions — a soft-money ban, equalized contribution limits, and a $100,000 cap on House candidates' personal contributions — never became law in the 105th Congress [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National party committees and the wealthy donors, corporations, and unions who fund them: the unlimited soft-money channel stayed open for another two years, and no disclosure or limit was ever attached to it.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban soft money and cap candidate self-funding; it was referred to committee the same day and never advanced

for.name: 1 House Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it nominal bipartisan sponsorship

against.name: House Committee on House Oversight

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 21, 1997 and never held a hearing or marked it up; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, so it never drew enough support on either side to force a party-line fight; no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: Soft money was the parties' largest unregulated funding source; the ban would end it and subject nearly all party election spending to limits and public disclosure. Parties' interest in keeping the channel open ran directly against voters' interest in knowing who pays.

industries.industry: Wealthy donors, corporations, and unions giving soft money
industries.note: The bill eliminates their ability to give unlimited, largely undisclosed money to party committees to influence federal elections, replacing it with capped, disclosed contributions.

They lose the ability to route soft money into federal elections, but the bill preserves State Party Grassroots Funds for voter registration, generic campaign activity, and purely state and local work.
The multicandidate PAC limit would drop from $5,000 to $2,500 per election, equalizing PACs with individual donors; individual donors, by contrast, would see their limit triple.
